The International Monetary Fund has warned on Hong Kong banks’ rising mainland exposure in a review of the city's economy published on Tuesday. 

The IMF said that Hong Kong banks’ lending to mainland firms and individuals has risen to 19 per cent of their total assets. The figure excludes loans to mainland banks.

“While deepening integration suggests that financial linkages will continue to grow, the large exposure requires close monitoring and cooperation with mainland supervisors,” said the IMF in the report, citing slowing mainland economic growth, rising US interest rates and the possibility asset price shocks.

The Bank for International Settlements says there is US$430 billion in loans outstanding from Hong Kong banks to mainland entities. However, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority clarifies that US$320 billion of this figure relates to routine interbank debt, such as loans from Hong Kong banks to their mainland subsidiaries. Only US$110 billion of that total relates to non-bank debts, said the HKMA.

“Therefore, the US$430 billion figure includes normal bank lending activities and support for mainland companies operating in China. The HKMA doesn't think this is hot money,” said Yokee Wong, an HKMA spokesman.

GSG View

Gazing out across the park and lake at the distant view of Taunton's magnificent cathedral-like church, it is hard to believe the school is only one mile from the station (two hours to London) and ten minutes from the College. The central house – a handsome and homely 18th century building – is the focal point around which the school operates. The original stable block now forms part of a delightfully intimate courtyard with rose bushes and inviting benches for chatting in the summer. Over the years, brightly coloured and airy dorms have been added with clever partitioning, affording privacy without separation. (Do make sure you see the boys' bathroom, marvellously painted with jungle scenes for aspiring Mowglis and with admonitions on hygiene for young 21st century Stalkys cleverly woven in.)

 Separate common-rooms for boys and girls are delightfully furnished with areas for more private conversation, while children can munch on the fresh fruit provided. Accessible library in the original house – elegant but functional. Terrific art and very popular drama in the theatre. Well-equipped labs and lively teaching. Excellent computer facilities. Riding is very popular and plans for fishing in the recently-purchased lake. A wide variety of games are played to a high standard, with success in national and regional competitions. Good modern sports hall, outdoor heated pool, 10 tennis courts and three netball courts. An interesting range of hobbies offered on a daily basis. Pupils are kept busy.

 Several things make King's Hall special. Taking advantage of their rural surroundings, there is an exciting Forest School in the grounds, complete with leafy huts for pow-wows and areas for cooking over wood fires: a wonderful place for simply mucking around and being children. Also the Pelican Pals, boys and girls in year 7 sporting their distinctive red caps who go out and play with younger children, really getting to know them and frequently offering comfort, encouragement and advice. We watched some in action with the tinies on the superb Astroturf: it was impossible to tell who was enjoying it more. Prefects have given way to Pelicans – a big improvement, leading to humane and considerate leadership. All of year 8 then play a part in helping to run the school.

 Weekend activities are popular – one mother told us it was virtually impossible to persuade her child to come home on Sundays – and all boarding staff, led by charismatic houseparents, are fully involved. The nursery and pre-prep are delightfully housed in what look like log cabins, adding a sense of adventure and discovery. That is the overall feeling we had about the school. The children are obviously happy with the considerate challenges they are set and the encouragement they receive; that is reflected in their sunny friendliness, on which sit the good old-fashioned virtues of courtesy and consideration.

 Generous arrangements are available for Forces families and scholarships, open to all, are awarded at 11+. They continue through the College, subject to annual review.

 Not a slick or sophisticated school – not a county school with over-riding social pretensions, but a place where children can mature at their own pace, enjoy their surroundings, have a lot of fun and know they will be ready for their next school. Indeed we met a number at their next school, who looked back on their days at King's Hall with huge affection and gratitude. One told us she had 'never been happier in her life,' but added thoughtfully, 'Mind you, in those days, I didn't have A levels to worry about'.

Bruton School for Girls welcomes overseas students into Sunny Hill Preparatory School (from age 7) into the Senior School (from age 11) and the Sixth Form (16+).

Senior School Applications – One Year or More
The School is a UKiset associate school. Students shall complete the Student Profile form from the UKiset website. This will be sent to the School as part of the student's UKiset profile package and used with his/her UKiset results to assess their application to Bruton School for Girls.

After the student has taken the test and we have received their UKiset profile package we will decide if we are able to proceed with the application. At which point we will ask you to complete a school Registration form and pay the registration fee of £50. We will then apply for the relevant school references and any other information we may need to support your application, and arrange for the student to have a Skype interview with our Headmistress.

Prep School Entry
The School does not expect candidates applying for a place in the Prep School to take the UKiset test. For entry to the Prep School, we ask candidates to sit age appropriate assessments in English and Maths.

Short Stay Students
We accept applications (space permitting) for short stay students for a minimum of one term. For short stay students applications are considered on an individual basis, and may involve some entrance testing.

Registration
To register your daughter for a place at Bruton School for Girls we require a completed Registration Form, payment of the £50 Registration Fee, a copy of the front page of her passport and copies of her most recent school reports.

Entrance Criteria
Entry to Bruton School for Girls is dependent upon the following:
- Current school reports/school reference
- Successful completion of UKiset test or School entrance tests (English and Maths) for Prep School and Short Stay applicants.
- Subject specific assessments if required

Offer and Acceptance of a Place
An offer of a place at Bruton School for Girls is made by the Headmistress or Head of the Prep School in writing. To accept a place we ask you to return the signed Acceptance Form and payment of the deposit of £500. Please ensure that any bank charges levied are covered so that the full £500 deposit is received by the school.

Visas
For those students who require a visa to study in the UK, the School will issue a Confirmation of Acceptance for Study (CAS) directly to the UK Visa & Immigration Service (UKVI).

There is a wholesomeness about Malvern for those who lift their eyes to the hills that can balance the daily busyness. The offshoots in China and Egypt will add to the global dimension and set everyone looking to the far horizons - not just at the opportunities but also, we hope, at the challenges. * 80% are boarders, and all are full
*  About half of those taking IB achieve over 40 points (average school point score 35 in 2014)
* sixth form is split more or less exactly in half between IB and A level

* The school is very cosmopolitan in feel and outlook – about 30% are from overseas, and there are about 40 different nationalities represented at the moment.
* The atmosphere felt well-disciplined without being too formal
* Among the alumni of the college are at least two Commonwealth prime ministers, two Nobel prize winners, an Olympic Gold medallist and many other notables from the worlds of science, law, the military, business, politics, sports and literature - including CS Lewis
* nine to Oxbridge in 2014, About a third go on to US, Canada and mainland Europe top institutions
* In recent years the majority of applicants have won places at Russell Group universities and well over 75% (90% in 2013) are accepted at their first choice universities every year 
* have a trained team of US admissions counsellors who help any potential US applicant through the procedure from start to finish. Pupils are required to sit SATs (standardised admissions tests) for entry and Malvern is now a SAT centre offering the test six times a year 
* Pupils who wish to apply to any other non-UK university (this year, we have applicants to Australia, Hong Kong, Germany, the Netherlands, Canada, Italy, Switzerland and Shanghai) benefit from advice from the school's Head of International University Admissions
* Eight applicants will take up places at Oxbridge, whilst London proved, once again, to be the favourite destination, attracting 18 applicants (amongst them 7 to UCL, 6 to KCL and 4 to Imperial). Others: including the University of Pennsylvania (in the 'Ivy League'), Stern Business School, University of Miami, New York University and McGill. In Europe, pupils took up places at the School of Economics at the Università Bocconi in Italy, and universities in Madrid, Amsterdam and Istanbul, and the European Business School in Frankfurt, Germany. 
* Malvern College’s first international campus, Malvern College Qingdao, opened in September 2012.  

GSG View

This is a school for the international set, and those who come from the local area, or even ‘over the hill’ - as the other side of the Malverns is described - undoubtedly benefit by having their horizons expanded beyond the comfortable values of the English shires. There are huge opportunities for pupils to learn from different cultures here and the college does well to work on its links with the local community, so it is not just the moneyed international culture that pupils assimilate, delightfully appealing though that is. There is a wholesomeness about Malvern for those who lift their eyes to the hills that can balance the daily busyness. The offshoots in China and Egypt will add to the global dimension and set everyone looking to the far horizons - not just at the opportunities but also, we hope, at the challenges. This is a school deeply bedded in the British public school tradition but with its sights now set across the globe to prepare the pupils for world citizenship.

School is listening and has taken note.

[Sep14] Candidates unable to attend a Test and Interview Day will be expected to sit a general Maths and either a general English paper, for candidates with English as their first language, or an EAL paper, for candidates for whom English is not their first language. The entrance papers are designed to test skills and potential rather than factual recall.

The Maths paper, which covers a range of different topics, gives candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their problem solving ability; candidates need to be familiar with manipulating fractions and decimals, and have met Pythagoras theorem, trigonometry and simultaneous equations. The stronger candidates may, for
example, have learned to solve quadratic equations.

The English paper requires the analysis of either a piece of unseen prose or poetry and we are looking for the quality of ideas candidates put forward in terms of characterisation, features of language and their ability to identify themes.

The EAL paper is designed to test a candidate’s ability to communicate in written English. The test comprises vocabulary and grammatical exercises and an extended writing opportunity at the end of the paper.

Overseas candidates unable to come to the school for a Test and Interview Day will be expected to make arrangements to sit the entrance papers at their current school, or at some other independent venue. The papers will be sent out in early November, together with a reference request from the candidate's current school, for return to us by 14 Nov (Fri). A Skype interview with the Head and/or the Director of Admissions may then be arranged depending upon the results of the entrance papers.

Our process and deadlines are outlined below:
 
By 31 January 2018:
Complete the application form and return it to admissions@radley.org.uk with the entry fee of £250.  Bank transfer details can be found on the application form (parents need to use their son's name as a reference with their payment).  If their son is a potential music or sport scholar they will also need to complete the relevant music or sport form and return it to admissions@radley.org.uk
 
By 9 February 2018:
 
Boys must have sat the ISEB CPT
Need to receive report from boy's school. School report format attached. 
Ukiset results required (if this has been sat)
Music and/or Sport Form with relevant music and sport references attached (only required if boys are of scholarship standard)
 
 
We will write to parents at the end of March 2018 to let them know whether their son has been shortlisted for one of our Assessment Days.  Our Assessment days will take place on 26 April, 3 May, 8 May and 10 May 2018.  If a shortlisted boy has not yet visited Radley, we would be happy to arrange a tour the day before his Assessment day.

*  Boys applying from state schools sit Radley’s own entrance papers instead of CE.
*  Boys are admitted to Radley from the age of 13. They may be added to the entry lists from birth and it is advisable to enter a boy’s name as early as possible. A registration fee of £100 is charged for putting a boy’s name down on the registration lists * Boys join the School in September and should be under 14 on the 31st of August in the year of entry. Boys will only be admitted after their fourteenth birthday in exceptional circumstances.
* Three years before a boy is due to come a Final Acceptance Form
* Around 30 to 35 places are reserved each year for the Warden’s List.  This is a method of entry for boys who are not offered a place from our waiting lists or who are too late to register at all.
* Foundation awards, need to take entrance test in Eng and Maths on 28th Nov 15, sample papers are available.
* There are a few places available in the 6th form each year. These are awarded as a result of examinations and interviews held at Radley in the November before entry
